pa_beam_rocks.blurb: A compact cliff on the Laurel Highlands ridge in Forbes State Forest, tall by Pennsylvania standards at roughly 70 feet. It mixes a handful of bolted and trad lines with a lively field of boulder problems at the base, right beside the long-distance hiking trail. Most of the problems fall between VB and V4, with a few harder ones, and the rope lines run from 5.5 to 5.11. The rock is on the soft side and the cliff stays shady, so it can hold moisture and is best saved for a dry spell. The walk from the road is short and easy, about five minutes on a wide track, and the place gets busy on pleasant weekends.
pa_beam_rocks.approach: A wide, gently graded track leads from the roadside lot to the top of the cliff; the base is reached by a trail that drops down beside the boulders.

pa_squirrel_rock_bouldering.blurb: A collection of boulders in the wooded hills behind Mocanaqua, an old coal-mining area where culm banks and abandoned workings still mark the landscape. This is the biggest bouldering zone in the neighborhood, with problems that cover a very wide spread: plenty in the V1 to V4 range, a solid group from V5 to V7, and a few serious lines into double digits. The boulders have slabs, roofs, arêtes and cracks, and several lines are tall enough that spotters and extra pads make a real difference. Plan on a loop of different boulders rather than one concentrated block.

pa_main_area_6.blurb: The core of Coll's Cove, a spread-out boulderfield of fine-grained gritty sandstone in southwestern Pennsylvania, often compared with nearby Cooper's Rock for its quality. Nearly every boulder holds at least one good line, and the problems here range from VB to V12: a broad middle in the V2 to V5 range, plus a notable cluster of harder lines from V6 up that makes it a good place to project. Boulders are scattered through woods, so expect some walking between them, and bring several pads. The rock tends to feel best in cool, dry weather.

pa_main_area_4.blurb: The central boulderfield of Falls City Boulders, known locally as The Pyle, spread across a wooded hillside above Ohiopyle. The sandstone is gritty and can be sharp on the skin, but the quality is high and it is the most developed bouldering in the park. Problems run from V1 up to V12, with the bulk between V3 and V7 and some tall lines with committing topouts. The boulders are reached by about a mile of mostly flat hiking on the long-distance trail out of town, so pack light and bring enough pads for the walk.
pa_main_area_4.approach: About a mile of mostly level walking on the Laurel Highlands Trail from the Falls City end of Ohiopyle; the boulders sit just off the path.

pa_beam_rocks_climbs.blurb: The climbing at the base of Beam Rocks on the Laurel Highlands ridge: a tidy set of boulder problems that spills out below a roughly 70-foot cliff, with a couple of trad lines added. Problems cover the full beginner range, with a lot of VB to V3, and a few harder ones near V5 and V6. The base sits alongside the hiking trail, so hikers pass through, and the stone is softer and shaded enough to stay damp after rain. Some of the taller problems are on the western side, so bring a spotter and pads.

pa_bouldering_2.blurb: A patch of sandstone boulders scattered beneath a small sport cliff near Connellsville. The set is modest in size but strong in quality, and it stands out for its high concentration of harder lines: V4 is the most common single grade, and nearly half the problems are V7 or harder, with a few V10 and above. Easier problems exist but are in short supply. Some lines are clean while others need brushing, and weekends can feel crowded. The walk in is about ten minutes on wooded trail.
pa_bouldering_2.approach: A wooded trail climbs from the road to the boulders, passing a creek and then following a logging track to the rocks.

pa_moby_s_and_friends.blurb: One of the larger sectors at Governor Stable, a boulder field of dark diabase in northern Lancaster County. The blocks are good quality, with lines packed close together so a lot of climbing fits in a single day. Most problems are V0 to V3, with a handful around V5 and one much harder line. Landings are sometimes flat, but pads are still wise. The boulders sit in a sheltered hollow that catches the sun and can run noticeably warmer than the surrounding countryside, which makes it a pleasant place on cool, bright days and a hot one in summer.

qc_la_source_bouldering.blurb: This is a low cliff, roughly eight or nine meters tall and a few hundred meters long, in the Kékéko hills of Abitibi near Rouyn-Noranda. Several sectors are equipped with bolts, so most of the climbing is sport and top-rope, mostly between 5.9 and 5.12, with some trad lines and a smaller set of boulder problems from V0 to V5. First bolts are placed high, so a stick-clip helps. Because the top can be reached on foot, easy top-rope setups are possible. The forest around it is northern taiga.

qc_right_of_pond.blurb: The main sector of Julien-Labedan, a small crag in the Laurentides north of Montreal. It holds most of the routes at the crag, and they are largely trad with a few sport lines, mostly in the 5.9 to 5.11 range with some easier lines from 5.6 and a few harder ones. A clear open area stretches along the base, and the top is easy to walk to, so setting up a top-rope is straightforward. It is a good place for a short day of moderate climbing, and weekends can be busy, with the easier lines drawing the biggest crowds.
